newsitem.title: USA: Brisk April placements boost US fed cattle numbers.
newsitem.headline: Brisk April placements boost US fed cattle numbers.

text.p: Lower corn prices and enticing profit margins encouraged cattle feeders to place greater numbers of cattle on feed during April than a year earlier, livestock analysts said.
The U.S. Agriculture Department is expected to confirm the larger numbers on Friday in its monthly Cattle on Feed report, set for release at 1400 CDT/1900 GMT.

Analysts project the data will show total cattle on feed in feedlots of 1,000 head or more capacity in the seven key states on May 1 at an average 109.6 percent of a year ago. Analyst estimates ranged from 108.0 to 111.0 percent.

"The report is going to confirm what we have been anticipating - cattle-on-feed numbers, percentage wise, continue to grow in relation to a year ago," said Joe Kropf of Kropf and Love Consulting, who was looking for on-feed numbers at 111 percent of last year.

Analysts said placements were light last year which resulted in a wide range of placement estimates for April this year. Estimates averaged 113.9 percent of a year ago in a Reuter pre-report survey, ranging from 104.9 to 127.5 percent.
Analysts continue to estimate seven-state numbers while building historical data on the 12-state part of the report.
USDA made revisions to its seven-state report and introduced a 12-state report in January 1996.

"The cattle feeder had a quite good feeding margin in April and the corn market was well below a year ago. They were marketing good and making money" giving them incentive to put more cattle on feed, Kropf said.

"Last year we had 7.8 million head and our number for this year is almost 8.5 million head," said Jim Robb with the Livestock Marketing Information Center in Denver, Colo., which estimated on-feed supplies at 109 percent of last year.
But some analysts said placements were only up slightly from a year earlier in April as profit margins were squeezed by rising feeder cattle prices.

"There was an element of competition for the feeder cattle in the month of April that didn't exist a month earlier than that, and that limited the placements during the month," said Chuck Levitt, senior analyst for Alaron Trading Corp. He forecast April placements at 105.7 percent of a year earlier.
Others agreed that high feeder prices limited placements.
"Breakevens were not that good against the summer and still not that great from what the feeder cattle prices are," said Karl Skold, director of research for Frontier Risk Management.
April marketings estimates averaged 101.0 percent of a year ago, ranging from 98.6 to 104.0 percent.
Feedlots continued to keep marketings current during the month, but there are more cattle ahead and the marketing pace will have to continue strong, analysts said.

"If this market is going to have much strength anytime this spring or summer, after the next week or so, it will have to come from the demand side. There will be no shortage of cattle or beef supplies," Kropf added.
